summary: This topic explores the disciplined methods used to discover, analyze, specify, validate, and manage software requirements. It details the essential taxonomy of requirements: Business Requirements (high-level organizational goals), User Requirements (operational user tasks), Functional Requirements (system behaviors, services, and transformations), and Non-Functional Requirements (quality attributes and operational constraints such as response time, availability, security, and reliability). The five core requirements engineering activities — Inception/Feasibility, Elicitation (interviews, surveys, workshops), Analysis and Negotiation (MoSCoW prioritization), formal Specification (IEEE 830 SRS, User Stories with INVEST criteria), and Validation (verifiability, consistency, completeness) — are examined. Uncontrolled Scope Creep and Requirements Traceability Matrices (RTM) connecting requirements to downstream design, code, and test artifacts are thoroughly analyzed.

key_terms.definition: A statement specifying a function, behavior, or service that the software system must actively provide or execute.
A statement specifying constraints, operational qualities, or performance benchmarks (e.g., security, reliability, latency) that the system must satisfy.
The formal document that completely describes the intended behavior, interfaces, and constraints of a software system.
The gradual, uncontrolled expansion of a project's scope beyond its original baseline without corresponding adjustments to budget, time, or resources.
A grid mapping each functional and non-functional requirement to its originating stakeholder need, architectural component, and verifying test cases.
A concise requirement description written from an end-user perspective: 'As a [role], I want [feature], so that [benefit]', supported by acceptance criteria.
An initial investigation determining whether a proposed system is cost-effective, practically achievable, and legally compliant before project funding.
The characteristic of a requirement stating that it can be conclusively proved or measured by a finite, cost-effective testing procedure.

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Questions 5 & 18: What type of software requirement specifies system constraints such as reliability, response time, and availability?
options: Non-functional requirement
Functional requirement
User requirement
Domain requirement
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements specify quality attributes, behavioral constraints, and operational standards (e.g., response time under load, 99.9% uptime reliability, data encryption security). Functional requirements, by contrast, specify the specific services and calculations the system must perform.

why_wrong.1: Functional requirements describe what the system does (features, calculations), not how well or under what constraints it does it.
why_wrong.2: User requirements can be either functional or non-functional, written in non-technical language.
why_wrong.3: Domain requirements reflect fundamental operational laws of the application domain (e.g., banking regulations).

marking_points: Identifies Non-functional requirement as specifying constraints like reliability and response time
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Questions 5 & 18

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 6: What does a feasibility study in requirements engineering primarily determine?
options: The cost-effectiveness, technical practicality, and viability of the proposed system
The exact variable names to be used in source code
The test case assertions for unit testing
The physical color scheme of the user interface
questions.explanation: A feasibility study is a short, focused investigation conducted before allocating full project budget to decide whether the proposed software is worth building. It assesses economic feasibility (cost vs benefit), technical feasibility (skills and tools), and operational practicality.

Variable naming is a detailed coding activity.
Test assertions are written during detailed design and implementation.
UI styling is decided during user-interface design.

marking_points: Cost-effectiveness and technical practicality
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 6

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 16: Which type of requirement specifies how the system should react to particular inputs and what services it must provide?
options: Functional requirement
Non-functional requirement
System constraint
Legal compliance requirement
questions.explanation: Functional requirements define the core functions of the software: input-to-output transformations, business rules, data processing, calculations, and specific feature capabilities (e.g. 'The system shall calculate late fee penalties at 5% per month').

why_wrong.1: Non-functional requirements describe operational constraints and quality attributes, not functional behaviors.
why_wrong.2: A constraint restricts design freedom (e.g. must run on Android 12).
why_wrong.3: Legal compliance is a category of non-functional constraint.

marking_points: Identifies Functional requirement as describing services and behavior
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 16

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 17: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a good software requirement?
options: Ambiguous
Verifiable
Traceable
Consistent
questions.explanation: Ambiguity is the single most dangerous defect in requirements engineering! A good requirement must be clear, unambiguous (having exactly one possible interpretation), verifiable, complete, consistent, and traceable. An ambiguous requirement inevitably leads to developer misinterpretation.

why_wrong.1: Verifiability is an essential quality of good requirements.
why_wrong.2: Traceability is an essential quality of good requirements.
why_wrong.3: Consistency (no mutual contradictions) is an essential quality of good requirements.

marking_points: Selects Ambiguous as an undesirable defect, not a good characteristic
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 17

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 19: What are Business Requirements primarily concerned with?
options: The high-level purpose, strategic goals, and business justification of the project
The exact SQL syntax for database tables
The hardware clock speed of developer laptops
The memory layout of C language structs
questions.explanation: Business requirements define the organization's overarching vision and commercial/institutional rationale: why the system is being funded, what problem it solves, and how return on investment or organizational efficiency will be measured.
marking_points: Strategic purpose, goals, and business justification
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 19

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 20: Which category of requirements describes the operational tasks and high-level workflows that end-users can perform with the software?
options: User requirements
Compiler directives
Assembly instructions
Hardware constraints
questions.explanation: User requirements are written from the perspective of external actors, describing everyday tasks, operational workflows, and services provided to users without mandating low-level technical implementation details.
marking_points: Identifies User requirements
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 20

questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 49: What is 'Scope Creep' and why is it dangerous to software projects?
options: The unplanned, continuous expansion of project boundaries and requirements without proportional adjustments to time, budget, and resources.
A virus that slowly infects developer computers.
A decrease in the number of lines of code written per day.
The process of shrinking project features to finish ahead of schedule.
questions.explanation: Scope creep occurs when stakeholders continuously add features, tweaks, and new requests throughout development without formally increasing the budget or deadline. This leads directly to project delays, cost overruns, developer burnout, and architectural degradation.

why_wrong.A virus that slowly infects developer co: Confuses a managerial phenomenon with malware.
why_wrong.A decrease in code written per day: Metric of developer velocity, not scope creep.
why_wrong.The process of shrinking project feature: This is scope reduction or descoping, the opposite of scope creep.

marking_points: Unplanned expansion of project boundaries
Lack of proportional time/budget adjustment
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 49

questions.question: A client states in a requirements meeting: 'The university portal must be fast and user-friendly.' Why is this considered an unacceptable requirement in a formal SRS, and how should it be rewritten?
options: It is completely unverifiable and subjective; it must be quantified with measurable operational metrics (e.g. 'Under a load of 500 concurrent users, 95% of course registration requests shall complete within 2.0 seconds').
It is fine as written because developers know what 'fast' means.
It should be deleted because software performance does not matter.
It should be rewritten using binary assembly code.
questions.explanation: Vague adjectives like 'fast', 'robust', or 'intuitive' cannot be validated by a test suite because there is no pass/fail criterion. Requirements engineers must quantify non-functional requirements by specifying exact workloads, percentile response times, error rates, and testing environments.

Different developers will interpret 'fast' as 50ms, 2 seconds, or 10 seconds.
why_wrong.It should be deleted because performance: Performance is a critical non-functional requirement.
Requirements are written in natural language specifications, not machine code.

marking_points: Identifies subjective unverifiability
Quantifies workload and measurable response time
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 6.6

questions.question: What is a Functional Requirement?
questions.answer: A statement specifying what services, functions, and behaviors the system must actively provide.
questions.explanation: Describes system behavior and data transformations.
marking_points: Specifies services and behaviors system must provide
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 6

questions.question: What is a Non-Functional Requirement?
questions.answer: A constraint on the services or functions offered by the system, covering quality attributes such as performance, reliability, security, and usability.
questions.explanation: Tested in Nile Exam Q5 & Q18.
marking_points: Constraints on services/functions; quality attributes
questions.source: Nile Exam Q5 & Lecture Notes Section 6

questions.question: What are the five core activities of Requirements Engineering?
questions.answer:
1. Inception & Feasibility Study
2. Elicitation
3. Analysis & Negotiation
4. Specification (SRS)
5. Validation
marking_points: Feasibility, Elicitation, Analysis, Specification, Validation
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 6.1

questions.question: What are five essential characteristics of a good software requirement?
marking_points: Unambiguous, Verifiable, Complete, Consistent, Traceable

questions.question: What is Scope Creep?
questions.answer: The uncontrolled expansion of product requirements and project scope during development without adjustments to schedule, budget, or resources.
marking_points: Uncontrolled scope expansion without time/budget adjustment

questions.question: What is a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)?
questions.answer: A table mapping each requirement ID to its source business need, architectural component, implementation code, and validating test cases.
questions.explanation: Ensures full lifecycle coverage and impacts analysis.
marking_points: Maps requirements to design, code, and test cases
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 6.5

questions.question: What is the standard template for writing an Agile User Story?
questions.answer: 'As a [type of user], I want [a capability/feature], so that [a specific business benefit].'
marking_points: As a... I want... so that...
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 6.4

questions.question: What does the MoSCoW prioritization acronym stand for?
questions.answer:
- Must have (mandatory)
- Should have (high priority, non-critical)
- Could have (desirable if time permits)
- Won't have (deferred to future releases)
questions.explanation: Commonly used in agile requirements negotiation.
marking_points: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have

case_studies.scenario: Nile University commissions a new online continuous assessment and examination portal. During initial discovery, the university registrar provides only a two-page bulleted list containing statements like: 'The portal must be user-friendly', 'The system should be extremely fast during peak exam weeks', and 'All student data must be secure'. Three months into development, faculty deans begin requesting automated timetable scheduling, SMS parents alerts, and biometric face verification, claiming these were 'obviously implied' in the original scope.

sub_questions.question: What two critical requirements engineering deficiencies caused this project crisis?
options: Vague, unverifiable requirements in the original document, coupled with a lack of formal change control leading to severe scope creep.
Developers using Python instead of HTML.
The server running on 64-bit architecture instead of 32-bit.
Failure to install antivirus software on the campus routers.
sub_questions.explanation: The initial requirements suffered from ambiguity and lack of verifiability ('fast', 'secure', 'user-friendly'). Without a formal Software Requirements Specification (SRS), baseline sign-off, and a change control board, stakeholders added new features indiscriminately, resulting in classic scope creep.

Technology choices are irrelevant to the requirements governance breakdown.
Conflates network security with requirements management.

marking_points: Identifies unverifiable/ambiguous initial requirements
Identifies lack of change control and resulting scope creep

sub_questions.question: Apply the MoSCoW prioritization technique to negotiate and stabilize the scope of this university examination portal. Categorize the conflicting requirements.
sub_questions.answer:
1. MUST HAVE (Core Critical Path): Secure student login, online exam taking, automated score recording, and grade calculation.
2. SHOULD HAVE (Important but Workaround Possible): Automated PDF results generation and lecturer grade submission dashboards.
3. COULD HAVE (Desirable if Time Permits): SMS alerts to students/parents for exam schedule reminders.
4. WON'T HAVE (Deferred to Phase 2): Automated AI biometric face verification and complex multi-faculty automated timetable optimization algorithms.
sub_questions.explanation: MoSCoW allows stakeholders to agree on a viable baseline, preventing project collapse while acknowledging future desires.
marking_points: Must Have: Exam taking, secure login, score recording
Should Have: PDF results, lecturer dashboards
Could Have: SMS alerts
Won't Have: Biometric face verification and automated timetable scheduling

case_studies.scenario: A financial payment infrastructure provider in Nigeria is specifying the non-functional requirements (NFRs) for a real-time instant payment switch handling interbank settlements. System downtime during banking hours could destabilize commercial liquidity. The lead engineer must translate vague stakeholder desires into rigorous, measurable non-functional requirements for the SRS.

sub_questions.question: The banking client demands 'high availability'. What exact mathematical metric and industry standard benchmark should be written into the SRS for an enterprise payment switch?
sub_questions.answer: 99.99% availability (less than 52.6 minutes of downtime per year)
sub_questions.explanation: In financial infrastructure, 'high availability' is quantified using 'nines'. An availability SLA of 99.99% ('four nines') permits at most 52.6 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year, providing a clear mathematical pass/fail test for site reliability engineers.
marking_points: Quantifies availability as 99.99% (or 99.999%)
Specifies downtime threshold
sub_questions.source: Software Engineering Quality Metrics & Non-Functional Requirements

sub_questions.question: Write two fully verifiable, unambiguous non-functional requirements for this payment gateway: one for Performance Latency and one for Security Compliance.
sub_questions.answer:
1. Performance / Latency NFR: 'Under a continuous load of 2,000 transactions per second (TPS), 99% of payment settlement API responses shall complete with a round-trip latency of less than 500 milliseconds.'
2. Security / Confidentiality NFR: 'All sensitive cardholder payment data shall be encrypted in transit using TLS 1.3 with forward secrecy and at rest using AES-256 encryption, in strict compliance with PCI-DSS Level 1 standards.'
sub_questions.explanation: Both statements specify exact workloads, measurable metrics (TPS, ms, encryption standards), and clear testing criteria.
marking_points: Performance specifies workload (TPS), response time (<500ms), and percentile (99%)
Security specifies encryption standard (TLS 1.3 / AES-256) and compliance benchmark (PCI-DSS)
sub_questions.source: Software Engineering SRS Non-Functional Specification Standards
